cse-1997-b-57-a.approach: A one-to-one function picks a distinct image for each of the n domain elements in order, so count ordered selections of n out of m values: the falling factorial $m^{\underline n}$.

steps.title: Assign images in order
steps.body: $f(1)$ has $m$ choices, $f(2)$ has $m-1$ (must differ from $f(1)$), …, $f(n)$ has $m-n+1$ choices.

pitfalls: $m^n$ counts all functions, not just one-to-one ones.
$\binom{m}{n}$ ignores which domain element gets which image (that is part (c)).
cse-1997-b-57-a.verification: Check $m=3,n=2$: injective maps $\{1,2\}\to\{1,2,3\}$ are the 6 ordered pairs of distinct values, and $3!/1!=6$.

cse-1997-b-57-b.approach: Since $f$ is one-to-one, at most one $i$ maps to 1. Choose that $i$, then map the remaining $n-1$ elements injectively into the remaining $m-1$ values.

steps.title: Pick the preimage of 1
steps.body: Exactly one $i$ has $f(i)=1$ (injectivity forbids two). There are $n$ choices for $i$.

steps.title: Map the rest
steps.body:
The other $n-1$ domain elements go one-to-one into $\{2,\dots,m\}$ ($m-1$ values):
$$\frac{(m-1)!}{\big((m-1)-(n-1)\big)!}=\frac{(m-1)!}{(m-n)!}$$

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body:
$$n\cdot\frac{(m-1)!}{(m-n)!}$$
Equivalently, total minus those avoiding 1: $\frac{m!}{(m-n)!}-\frac{(m-1)!}{(m-1-n)!}$ (for $m>n$).

pitfalls: Do not multiply by more than $n$ — no two elements can both map to 1.

cse-1997-b-57-c.approach: A strictly increasing function is determined completely by its image set: any $n$-element subset of $\{1..m\}$, listed in increasing order, gives exactly one such $f$.

steps.title: Bijection with subsets
steps.body: If $f(1)<f(2)<\dots<f(n)$, the image is an $n$-subset of $\{1,\dots,m\}$. Conversely each $n$-subset, sorted, defines exactly one increasing $f$.

steps.title: Count subsets
steps.body:
$$\binom{m}{n}=\frac{m!}{n!\,(m-n)!}$$
(Equivalently: each image set appears in $n!$ injective functions, and exactly one of those orders is increasing: $\frac{m!/(m-n)!}{n!}$.)

pitfalls: Answering $m!/(m-n)!$ counts all orders of the chosen images, not only the increasing one.

cse-1997-b-58-a.approach: Check reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of $E$ directly, each one inherited from a property of $R$ (reflexive, the symmetric definition of $E$, transitive).

steps.title: Reflexive
steps.body: For every $a\in A$, $(a,a)\in R$ since $R$ is reflexive. Both conditions of $E$ hold with $b=a$, so $(a,a)\in E$.

steps.title: Symmetric
steps.body: If $(a,b)\in E$ then $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,a)\in R$. The same two facts read in the other order say $(b,a)\in E$.

steps.title: Transitive
steps.body: Let $(a,b)\in E$ and $(b,c)\in E$. Then $(a,b),(b,c)\in R\Rightarrow(a,c)\in R$ and $(c,b),(b,a)\in R\Rightarrow(c,a)\in R$ by transitivity of $R$. Hence $(a,c)\in E$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $E$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation on $A$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Proof: $E$ is reflexive (from $R$ reflexive), symmetric (its definition is symmetric in $a,b$) and transitive (apply transitivity of $R$ in both directions).

pitfalls: Transitivity must be shown for both $(a,c)$ and $(c,a)$ — it needs transitivity of $R$ twice.
cse-1997-b-58-a.verification: Example: $R=\le$ on integers gives $E$ = equality, an equivalence relation, as expected.

cse-1997-b-58-b.approach: First show the relation does not depend on the chosen representatives (so $E_1\le E_2$ iff $(a,b)\in R$ for ALL $a\in E_1,b\in E_2$), then reflexivity and transitivity come from $R$ and antisymmetry from the definition of $E$.

steps.title: Representatives do not matter
steps.body: Suppose $(a,b)\in R$ with $a\in E_1,b\in E_2$, and take any $a'\in E_1,b'\in E_2$. Then $(a',a)\in R$ and $(b,b')\in R$ (definition of $E$), so by transitivity $(a',a),(a,b),(b,b')\in R\Rightarrow (a',b')\in R$.

steps.title: Reflexive
steps.body: For a class $E_1$ pick $a\in E_1$; $(a,a)\in R$, so $E_1\le E_1$.

steps.title: Antisymmetric
steps.body: Let $E_1\le E_2$ and $E_2\le E_1$. Take $a\in E_1,b\in E_2$; by the first step $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,a)\in R$, so $(a,b)\in E$: $a$ and $b$ are in the same class, i.e. $E_1=E_2$.

steps.title: Transitive
steps.body: Let $E_1\le E_2$, $E_2\le E_3$. Fix $a\in E_1,b\in E_2,c\in E_3$; by the first step $(a,b),(b,c)\in R$, so $(a,c)\in R$, giving $E_1\le E_3$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $\le$ is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on the equivalence classes of $E$: a partial order. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Proof: $\le$ is well defined independent of representatives; reflexive from $R$ reflexive, transitive from $R$ transitive, and antisymmetric because mutual $R$-relation puts elements in the same $E$-class.

pitfalls: Without the representative-independence step, transitivity fails: the witnesses $b$ for $E_1\le E_2$ and $E_2\le E_3$ may differ.
Antisymmetry needs $E_1=E_2$ as classes, not $a=b$ as elements.
cse-1997-b-58-b.verification: Collapsing the cycles of a preorder (e.g. reachability in a directed graph → its condensation DAG) gives exactly this partial order.

cse-1997-b-59-a.approach: $F$ counts monotone lattice paths: $F(n,m)=\binom{n+m}{n}$, which satisfies both the base case and Pascal's rule. Put $m=2$.

steps.title: Guess the closed form
steps.body: Try $G(n,m)=\binom{n+m}{n}$. Base: if $n=0$ or $m=0$, $G=\binom{m}{0}$ or $\binom{n}{n}=1$ ✓.

steps.title: Check the recurrence
steps.body: With $N=n+m$, $k=n$: $\binom{N}{n}=\binom{N-1}{n}+\binom{N-1}{n-1}=G(n,m-1)+G(n-1,m)$ ✓. So $F=G$.

cse-1997-b-59-b.approach: Match the recurrence to Pascal's rule: $\binom{n+m}{n}$ equals 1 when either argument is 0 and splits exactly as $F$ does.

steps.title: Recursive case
steps.body:
$$\binom{n+m}{n}=\binom{n+m-1}{n}+\binom{n+m-1}{n-1}=\binom{n+(m-1)}{n}+\binom{(n-1)+m}{n-1}$$
which is $F(n,m-1)+F(n-1,m)$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: $$F(n,m)=\binom{n+m}{n}=\frac{(n+m)!}{n!\,m!}$$

cse-1997-b-59-b.shortcut: $F(n,m)$ counts paths from $(n,m)$ to an axis taking unit steps left/down — the classic $\binom{n+m}{n}$ grid-path count.

cse-1997-b-59-c.approach: Write the call-count recurrence $C(n,m)=1+C(n-1,m)+C(n,m-1)$ with $C=1$ at the base, and notice $C=2F-1$ satisfies it (a full binary recursion tree with $F$ leaves has $2F-1$ nodes).
concepts: Full binary tree: leaves vs nodes

steps.title: Call-count recurrence
steps.body: Base ($n\le0$ or $m\le0$): $C=1$. Otherwise $C(n,m)=1+C(n-1,m)+C(n,m-1)$.

cse-1997-b-59-c.shortcut: Every non-base call has exactly 2 children, so the recursion tree is a full binary tree; its leaves each return 1, so #leaves $=F(n,m)$ and #nodes $=2F-1$.
pitfalls: Counting only the leaves ($F$) or forgetting the original call.

cse-1997-b-60-a.approach: Strong induction on $h$: a tree of height $h$ has one subtree of height $h-1$ (≥ $2^{h-1}$ nodes); the balance condition forces the other subtree to have at least $2^{h-1}-1$ nodes.

steps.title: Base h = 0
steps.body: A tree of height 0 is a single node: $1=2^0$ nodes ✓.

steps.title: Hypothesis
steps.body: Assume every size-balanced tree of height $h-1$ has at least $2^{h-1}$ nodes ($h\ge1$). Every subtree of a size-balanced tree is itself size-balanced.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body:
A tree $T$ of height $h$ has a subtree $T_1$ of height exactly $h-1$, so $|T_1|\ge2^{h-1}$. The other subtree $T_2$ satisfies $\big||T_1|-|T_2|\big|\le1$, so $|T_2|\ge2^{h-1}-1$.
$$|T|=1+|T_1|+|T_2|\ge1+2^{h-1}+2^{h-1}-1=2^h$$

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: By induction every size-balanced binary tree of height $h$ has at least $2^h$ nodes. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Proof by induction: base $h=0$ gives 1 node; for height $h$, one subtree has ≥ $2^{h-1}$ nodes and the other ≥ $2^{h-1}-1$, so total ≥ $1+2^{h-1}+2^{h-1}-1=2^h$.

pitfalls: The second subtree may have height less than $h-1$ — bound it through the size condition, not its height.
cse-1997-b-60-a.verification: The bound is tight: a perfect tree of height $h-1$ plus one extra leaf has $2^h$ nodes and is size-balanced.

cse-1997-b-60-b.approach: A size-balanced tree is complete except possibly the last level, so level $h-1$ is full: $2^{h-1}$ nodes.

steps.title: Levels above the last are full
steps.body: By induction: the subtrees of the root have sizes $k$ and $k$ or $k+1$. If their heights differ, the shorter one (height $h-2$, < $2^{h-1}$ nodes) and taller one (≥ $2^{h-1}$ nodes, part (a)) differ in size by 1, which forces sizes $2^{h-1}-1$ and $2^{h-1}$ — the shorter is perfect. So in every case all levels $0..h-1$ are full.

steps.title: Count level h − 1
steps.body: A full level at distance $h-1$ in a binary tree has $2^{h-1}$ nodes.

cse-1997-b-60-b.verification: $h=1$: root plus 1 or 2 children; distance 0 has $1=2^0$ node ✓. $h=2$ with 4 nodes: both root children exist → $2=2^1$ ✓.

cse-1997-b-61.approach: This is the two-pointer sliding window over positive numbers: keep $sum=A[i]+\dots+A[j]$; extend $j$ while $sum<M$, shrink from $i$ (recording the length) once $sum\ge M$.

steps.title: Invariant
steps.body: Window is $A[i..j]$ and $sum=\sum_{k=i}^{j}A[k]$. Initially $i=j=1$, so **line 3:** `Sum := A[1]`.

steps.title: Decide: grow or shrink
steps.body: Lines 7–11 extend the window (advance $j$), which is needed only when the window is too small. So **line 6:** `If sum < M then`. The else-branch (lines 15–17) runs when $sum\ge M$: it records length $j-i+1$ via $min=j-i$ and drops $A[i]$.

steps.title: Maintain the sum
steps.body: After `j := j + 1` the new element enters the window: **line 11:** `sum := sum + A[j]`.

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body: Because all $A[k]>0$, shrinking a window with $sum\ge M$ is the only way to find a shorter one, and growing is the only way to reach $M$. If no window ever reaches $M$, $min$ stays $n$ and $n+1$ is printed.

pitfalls: Line 6 as `sum >= M` swaps the meaning of the two branches.
Line 11 must add $A[j]$ after $j$ is incremented, not $A[j+1]$.
cse-1997-b-61.verification: Trace $A=[1,4,2],M=5$: sum=1<5 → j=2,sum=5 ≥5 → min=1, sum=4,i=2 → <5 → j=3,sum=6 → min stays 1, sum=2,i=3 → <5, j=n → finish; prints 2 (window [1,4] or [4,2]) ✓.

cse-1997-b-63-a.approach: S1 runs once per iteration of the while loop, and $t_2$ walks from the 2nd node to past the last node exactly once.

steps.title: Loop range
steps.body: $t_2$ starts at node 2 and moves one node per iteration (`t2 = t2->next` is unconditional) until it becomes NULL after node $n$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Iterations for nodes $2,3,\dots,n$: $n-1$. S1 is evaluated once per iteration, so $n-1$ comparisons. Note: the printed code writes `t1.val`/`t2.val`; read them as `t1->val`/`t2->val`.

cse-1997-b-63-b.approach: S2 executes once for every new distinct value met after the first node, so it ranges from 0 (all equal) to $n-1$ (all distinct).

steps.title: When S2 runs
steps.body: S2 runs exactly when $t_2$ holds a value different from the last kept node $t_1$ — i.e. at each position where the sorted list changes value.

steps.title: Minimum
steps.body: All $n$ elements equal: S1 is false every time → S2 runs **0** times.

steps.title: Maximum
steps.body: All elements distinct: S1 is true in all $n-1$ iterations → S2 runs **$n-1$** times.

cse-1997-b-63-c.approach: `*j` starts at 1 for the head and is incremented once per S2 (each new distinct value kept), so it ends as the number of distinct elements — the length of the de-duplicated list.

steps.title: Invariant
steps.body: After `*j = 1`, `*j` equals the number of nodes kept so far (head, then every node linked by `t1->next = t2`).

steps.title: At the end
steps.body: Kept nodes = one per distinct value, so `*j` = number of distinct elements = length of the resulting list (0 for an empty list, 1 for a single node).

answer.value: Number of distinct elements in the list (length of the resulting list)

cse-1997-b-64-a.approach: Count child pointers two ways: every node except the root is someone's child, and a node with $M$ keys has $M+1$ children.

steps.title: Children total
steps.body: Let $I$ = number of internal nodes. Every node except the root is a child of an internal node: total children $=(I+l)-1$.

steps.title: Keys total
steps.body: Node $x$ with $M_x$ keys has $M_x+1$ children, so $\sum M_x=\sum(\text{children}_x)-I=(I+l-1)-I=l-1$.

cse-1997-b-64-a.verification: A root with 1 key and 2 leaves: $l=2$, keys $=1=l-1$ ✓.

cse-1997-b-64-b.approach: To maximise internal nodes, give every node the minimum fan-out: non-root internal nodes need ≥ 4 keys = 5 children, root ≥ 2 children. Build level by level from the 52 leaves.
cse-1997-b-64-b.given:
| Node | Keys | Children |
|---|---|---|
| non-root internal | 4 – 8 | 5 – 9 |
| root | 1 – 8 | 2 – 9 |

steps.title: Parents of the leaves
steps.body: Each needs 5–9 children. Max nodes $=\lfloor52/5\rfloor=10$ (e.g. eight with 5 children, two with 6: $40+12=52$).

steps.title: Can the root sit on top?
steps.body: 10 children need 9 keys > $2d=8$, so no. Add a level: $\lfloor10/5\rfloor=2$ nodes of 5 children each.

steps.title: Root
steps.body:
2 children (1 key) is allowed for the root.
$$10+2+1=13$$

pitfalls: Using $\lceil52/5\rceil=11$ — 11 nodes would need ≥ 55 leaves.
Forgetting the root may have as few as 2 children.
cse-1997-b-64-b.verification: Any other split has ≤ 10 nodes above the leaves and then ≤ 2 above them, so 13 is the maximum.

cse-1997-b-64-c.approach: Minimise fan-out at every level: the root has at least 2 children and every other internal node at least $d+1$ children; leaves are all at depth $h$.

steps.title: Level counts
steps.body: Depth 0: 1 root. Depth 1: ≥ 2 nodes. Each internal node at depth $1..h-1$ has ≥ $d+1$ children, so depth $k$ has ≥ $2(d+1)^{k-1}$ nodes.

pitfalls: Using $d$ (keys) instead of $d+1$ (children) as the minimum fan-out.
Giving the root $d+1$ children — it may have only 2.
cse-1997-b-64-c.verification: $h=1$: root with 2 leaves → $2(d+1)^0=2$ ✓. Cross-check with (b): $d=4,h=3$ minimum leaves $=2\cdot25=50\le52$, consistent with the 3-level tree found there.

cse-1997-b-65.approach: Track two counters at once: $\#a \bmod 2$ and $\#b \bmod 3$. The product of a 2-state and a 3-state DFA gives 6 states, and all 6 are pairwise distinguishable, so 6 is minimum.

steps.title: States
steps.body: State $(i,j)$ means $\#a\equiv i \pmod 2$, $\#b\equiv j\pmod 3$: six states $(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2)$. Start = final = $(0,0)$.

scene.caption: Start state (0,0) is also the only accepting state.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.body:
| | on a | on b |
|---|---|---|
| $(i,j)$ | $(1-i,\,j)$ | $(i,\,(j+1)\bmod 3)$ |
The a-edges flip the row; the b-edges cycle along a row.

scene.caption: a toggles the a-parity (vertical), b advances the b-count mod 3 (horizontal cycle).

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: Two different states $(i,j)\ne(i',j')$ are distinguished by the suffix $a^{(2-i)\bmod2}b^{(3-j)\bmod3}$, which takes $(i,j)$ to $(0,0)$ (accept) but $(i',j')$ elsewhere (reject). So no two states merge: **6 states** is minimum.

answer.value: 6-state DFA: states $(i,j)$ with $i=\#a \bmod 2$, $j=\#b \bmod 3$; start and only final state $(0,0)$; on a: $(i,j)\to(1-i,j)$; on b: $(i,j)\to(i,(j+1)\bmod 3)$.

pitfalls: Building the two machines in sequence (concatenation) instead of in parallel (product).
Using 5 states (2+3) — that cannot remember both counts.

cse-1997-b-66.approach: Modify a DFA $M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$ for $L$. For prefixes, accept wherever an accepting state is still reachable; for reversal, flip every edge and swap start/final roles, giving an NFA.

steps.title: L^P: construction
steps.body: Let $F'=\{q\in Q : \exists w,\ \hat\delta(q,w)\in F\}$ (states that can still reach $F$). $M^P=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F')$.

steps.title: L^P: correctness
steps.body: $s\in L(M^P)\iff \hat\delta(q_0,s)\in F'\iff\exists s'\,:\,\hat\delta(q_0,ss')\in F\iff \exists s'\,:\,ss'\in L\iff s\in L^P$. $F'$ is computable by graph reachability, so $M^P$ is a finite automaton.

steps.title: L^R: construction
steps.body: Build NFA $N$: same states plus a new start $p_0$; for each $\delta(q,a)=r$ add the reversed edge $r\xrightarrow{a}q$; add $p_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f$ for every $f\in F$; the only final state is $q_0$.

steps.title: L^R: correctness
steps.body: $N$ has a path from $f\in F$ to $q_0$ labelled $a_k\cdots a_1$ exactly when $M$ has a path $q_0\to f$ labelled $a_1\cdots a_k$. So $N$ accepts $w^R$ iff $M$ accepts $w$, i.e. $L(N)=L^R$. By subset construction an NFA has an equivalent DFA, so $L^R$ is accepted by a finite state machine. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: For $L^P$: in the DFA for $L$, make final every state from which some final state is reachable. For $L^R$: reverse all transitions, make the old start state the only final state, and add a new start state with ε-moves to the old final states (an NFA, hence convertible to a DFA).

pitfalls: Making every state final for $L^P$ — dead states must stay non-final.
Reversing edges of a DFA gives an NFA in general; you must invoke subset construction (or NFA acceptance) to finish.
cse-1997-b-66.verification: $L=\{ab\}$: $L^P=\{\varepsilon,a,ab\}$ (states before the dead state become final) and $L^R=\{ba\}$ from the reversed path ✓.

cse-1997-b-67.approach: Encode precedence and associativity in the grammar levels: statements on top, `<` (lowest precedence, non-associative) above `+` (left-associative) above operands, and a left-recursive statement list for `begin … end`.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
```
S  → id := E
   | while E do S
   | begin SL end
SL → SL ; S | S
```
Each statement starts with a distinct token (`id`, `while`, `begin`), and `while … do S` has no `else`, so there is no dangling ambiguity.

steps.title: Expressions
steps.body:
```
E → T < T | T
T → T + F | F
F → id | num | ( E )
```
`<` sits at the lowest level (non-associative as in Pascal; `E → E < T | T` would also be unambiguous). `T → T + F` makes `+` left-associative and binds tighter than `<`.

steps.title: Why unambiguous
steps.body: Every expression has a unique split: the (at most one) top-level `<`, then the last top-level `+` in each side. Statement lists split only at `;` with left recursion, so each string has exactly one parse tree.

answer.value: S → id := E | while E do S | begin SL end;  SL → SL ; S | S;  E → T < T | T (or E → E < T | T);  T → T + F | F;  F → id | num | ( E )

pitfalls: Writing `E → E + E | E < E | id` is ambiguous (both precedence and associativity).
`SL → S ; SL | S ; SL` style rules with an empty alternative can create ambiguity with trailing `;`.
cse-1997-b-67.verification: `a + b < c + d` has the unique tree $(a+b) < (c+d)$; `a + b + c` parses only as $(a+b)+c$.

cse-1997-b-68.approach: Use synthesized attributes `code` (postfix string) and `type` (i or r) on every non-terminal; an operator node is integer only if both operands are integer, and emits its type-specific operator after its operands.

steps.title: Leaves
Multiplication and addition
Assignment
steps.body:
```
assign-stmt → LHS := E
   { assign.code := LHS.code || E.code || '(:=,' || LHS.type || ')' }
```
The assignment operator is typed by the target variable.

steps.title: Example
steps.body:
With `x:real, a,b:int`, `x := a + b * x` gives
`x a b x (*,r) (+,r) (:=,r)` — `b*x` is real because `x` is real, so the sum is real too.

answer.value: Synthesized attributes .code and .type: V→id {code=give-name(id); type=give-type(id)}; V→(E) copy; T→T1*V {type = i if both i else r; code = T1.code‖V.code‖(*,type)}; E→E1+T likewise with (+,type); unit rules copy; assign→LHS:=E {code = LHS.code‖E.code‖(:=,LHS.type)}.

pitfalls: Emitting the operator before the operands (prefix) instead of after.
Typing the assignment by the expression instead of the target variable.
cse-1997-b-68.verification: All-integer `i := j + k` yields `i j k (+,i) (:=,i)`, matching left-to-right postfix order.
